name: Amira Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, go for it. I've got opinions, so you might need to cut me off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small timber-frame firm, twelve of us. Half the week I'm in the yard helping build wall panels, studs and sheathing nailed up on a big table. The other half we truck them out and stand them up on site, mostly self-build houses and the odd school classroom. I'm still slow and my cuts aren't always square, but I love the day a house goes from slab to walls in two days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you've got opinions. What about the tech side of the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day, mostly to learn. When the lead hand shows me something, I go home and ask the chatbot why it's done that way, and it'll walk me through the maths. I share a flat with two friends, and I've got about ten days of money saved, so I can't afford to be wrong for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly. At work I'd say at least the planners can't blame the software for late deliveries anymore. Online I'd post something about how the money that went into the hype should've gone into housing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep learning the slow way, plus my chatbot. The firm lives order to order, and if the self-build market dips, they cut the newest people. That's me, and there's only one other timber firm within an hour's drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI to learn faster, because even a tool that's mostly hype explains a roof pitch better than my old maths teacher. I'd ask the boss if I can learn the panel-cutting saw in the yard. And I'd try to get a few weekend jobs fitting decking with a friend, for a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit restless. Like everyone got excited about a party and then it was just tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the firm cuts the newest people. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last February they had two weeks with no orders and sent me home without pay for both. I ate a lot of pasta and borrowed from my flatmate for the bus pass. I don't want to do that again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the job feel more secure, if AI isn't going to change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper contract with guaranteed hours in winter. Right now I'm paid by the day, and the day disappears whenever it rains or orders dry up. That's the thing that needs fixing, robots or not.

say: I'd say I'm **disappointed**, and the hype money should've gone into **housing**.
I'd joke that planners can't blame **software** for late deliveries anymore.
think: The firm lives **order to order** and cuts the newest people when orders dip.
There's only **one other** timber firm within an hour's drive.
do: Keep using **AI to learn** the maths behind each job.
Ask to learn the **panel-cutting saw** in the yard.
Pick up **weekend decking** jobs with a friend for a cushion.
feel: **Restless**, like expecting a party and getting tea.
S0.quote: Even a tool that's mostly hype explains a roof pitch better than my old maths teacher.
fieldNote: She treats AI as a **personal tutor**, not a threat.
Being **paid by the day** is her real insecurity.
Last February's **unpaid fortnight** still shapes her plans.
She'd add a **side income** even in a quiet world.

steps.text: Use the chatbot nightly to learn the maths behind each job
Ask the boss to train her on the panel-cutting saw
Fit decking on weekends with a friend for extra cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exciting if workers get a share of it. At work I'd tell everyone to learn the software before it learns them. Online I'd be the annoying one posting guides to free tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a timber-frame yard is basically a factory, so robots will come there first. The panels are made on a flat table, same shape every time. So either I'm the one who runs the machine, or I'm the one it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the boss straight out to put me on the new cutting line when they buy it, and offer to learn the software in my own time. I'd do the online course for the machine maker, the free one. And I'd get the union involved so the firm trains people rather than just hiring one engineer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buzzing and scared at the same time. Like the first time I used a nail gun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said either you run the machine or it replaces you. What decides which?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Speed, mostly, and whether the boss sees me as a learner or a pair of hands. The lead hand Kev is forty-eight and hates screens, so I think I've got a shot. I'd feel bad about Kev, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Kev in your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd go to site work, where the panels get stood up, because that's still hands-on for years. Honestly he'd be happier there. But he'd earn less without the yard overtime.

say: I'd say it's **exciting** if workers get a share.
I'd tell everyone to **learn the software** before it learns them.
think: **Timber-frame yards** are basically factories, so robots arrive there first.

S1.quote: A timber-frame yard is basically a factory, so robots will come there first.
fieldNote: She spots her firm's **yard work** as the most automatable part.

steps.text: Ask to run the new automated cutting line in the yard

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a four-day week and a basic income. At work I'd say the panel yard is already half a factory, so robots will be in by 2031 at the latest. Online I'd be organising, I think, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'd be fine until 2031 and then genuinely in trouble. I can run a machine, but if a robot can also install it, fix it and supervise it, what's left? I'd be thirty with no qualifications and ten days of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd get onto the cutting line and learn everything the AI planning side does, because I'd want to be the person who knows both. I'd try for a robotics technician course at the college, evenings. And I'd talk to my flatmates about moving somewhere cheaper so I can save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like riding a wave I'm actually good at, and then seeing the rocks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in your day between 2028 and 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drawings and the cutting lists would come straight from the AI, so nobody in the office would be checking them. I'd be the one spotting the mistakes on the table. For three years, that's actually a good job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you're adaptive and also that you'd be in trouble. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. Being adaptive gets me three good years, but I can't adapt my way out of a robot that adapts faster. That's where I'd need the government to step in.

say: I'd push for a **four-day week** and a **basic income**.
I'd tell the yard crew robots will be in **by 2031**.
think: She'd be fine **until 2031**, then genuinely in trouble.
With **no qualifications** and ten days saved, adapting has a limit.
do: Get onto the **cutting line** and learn the AI planning side too.
Start an evening **robotics technician** course at the college.
Talk to flatmates about **moving somewhere cheaper** to save.
feel: Like riding a **wave** she's good at, and then seeing the **rocks**.
S2.quote: I can't adapt my way out of a robot that adapts faster.
fieldNote: She expects **three good years** catching AI mistakes on the panel table.
She admits her **adaptability** only buys time.
Her politics shift from posting to **organising**.
She'd **cut rent** by moving with flatmates.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening robotics technician course at the college
Learn the AI planning software that sends cutting lists
Organise local campaigning for a four-day week
Move with her flatmates to a cheaper flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift, use it. At work I'd say the firm should be training all twelve of us now, not just me. Online I'd share the course links I'm using.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years plus three is enough to get properly qualified on the machines, and maybe the robots too. But I'm also realistic: if the robots fix themselves by 2034, technicians will shrink too. I'd still have to move up again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd do the technician course and get my carpentry papers at the same time, because the robot companies will want people who understand timber. I'd join the union's tech committee if they have one. And I'd save every penny from the yard overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, mostly, with a little cold spot in the middle of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the cold spot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money. If one bad winter wipes me out before I finish the course, all the plans go. Ten days of savings doesn't survive a February like last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone who'd help in that case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would lend a bit, but she's on a carer's wage herself. Mostly I'd ask the college about hardship grants. I'm not proud about asking, I'd just ask.

I'd tell the firm to train **all twelve** staff now.

feel: **Optimistic**, with a **cold spot** about money in the middle.
S3.quote: Ten days of savings doesn't survive a February like last year.
fieldNote: She pairs **timber knowledge** with machine skills as her edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a real plan, so no excuses. At work I'd say the young ones should be fine if we start now. Online I'd probably make videos about learning carpentry with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With thirteen years before the robots, I could be running a small crew by forty. Or doing machine setup, or both. It feels like enough runway if I don't do anything stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, carpentry papers and a start on the technician course. I'd try a small side thing, maybe making videos teaching basic joinery with AI help. And I'd keep pushing the union to make the firm pay for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. Like a long road trip where you know where the petrol stations are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned videos. Is that a real plan or a daydream?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half. My flatmate edits videos for a living and she said she'd help. If it makes fifty a month, that's my phone bill covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself at thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't get comfy. The robots are still coming, just later. Keep learning the next thing.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough for a real plan.
I'd tell young workers they're fine if we **start now**.
think: **Thirteen years** to robots lets her run a crew or set up machines by forty.
It's enough **runway** if she avoids big mistakes.

Keep pushing the union for **firm-paid training**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have three good years and then nothing to adapt to. What would help is free technician training, a guaranteed winter wage, and a basic income for the gap.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women in trades. Half the time I get the screen jobs because the men won't do them. That's going to be an advantage soon, and I find that quite funny.

headlineQuote: Half the time I get the screen jobs because the men won't do them.
portrait: Amira is **27**, a junior carpenter at a small **timber-frame** firm with ten days of savings.
She uses **AI daily** as a tutor and wants to run the yard's cutting machines.
She's **progressive**, pro-union and sees robots arriving in the yard first.
AGI by **2028** worries her because adapting only buys three years.
With **more time** she plans technician training, carpentry papers and a small video sideline.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because adapting gives her only three good **years**.
whatWouldHelp: Free **technician training**, a guaranteed winter wage and a **basic income** for the gap.
